rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God swears by the soul and its fashioning, then teaches it to recognize righteous and wicked deeds, a knowledge shared by ignorant and learned alike.
rows.anchor: أقسم بالنفس وخلقه لها ثم قال: فألهمها فجورها وتقواها، أي: فهمها أعمال البر وأعمال الفجور، حتى عرف ذلك الجاهل والعاقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To purify the soul is to make it grow and rise through obedience, righteousness, charity, and good works.
rows.anchor: قد أفلح من زكاها يريد أفلح من زكى نفسه، أي: أنماها وأعلاها بالطاعة والبر والصدقة واصطناع المعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root sense of purification is increase: crops yield abundantly and expenditure is blessed; zakat grows a person's wealth.
rows.anchor: وأصل التزكية: الزيادة، ومنه يقال: زكا الزرع يزكوا: إذا كثر ريعه، وزكت النفقة: إذا بورك فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A judge's endorsement of a witness is also called tazkiya because it raises the witness through accreditation and good repute.
rows.anchor: وتزكية القاضي للشاهد منه، لأنه يرفعه بالتعديل والذكر الجميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To bury the soul is to diminish and conceal it by abandoning good works and committing sins; the wicked hide themselves and lose dignity.
rows.anchor: وقد خاب من دساها، أي: نقصها وأخفاها بترك عمل البر، وبركوب المعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dassa is derived from dassastu, with one doubled s converted to y, as in labibt/labayt and qasaytu from qasasstu.
rows.anchor: ودساها: من دسست، فقلبت إحدى السينات ياء، كما يقال: لببت، والأصل لبيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab benefactors camped conspicuously on hills and lit night fires for visitors, while misers hid in recesses; their habits exemplify raising or burying the self.
rows.anchor: وكانت أجواد العرب تنزل الربا وأيفاع الأرض، لتشتهر أماكنها للمعتفين، وتوقد النيران في الليل للطارقين

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet praises a conspicuous, spacious home that feeds visitors, illustrating the virtue of making oneself known to those seeking hospitality.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر : وبوأت بيتك في معلم ... رحيب المباءة والمسرح كفيت العفاة طلاب القرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can omit a phrase when an earlier clause makes it clear; the omitted wording in this verse is signaled by its preceding mention of God's servants being sent.
rows.anchor: فحذفها، لأنه قال قبل: فإذا جاء وعد أولاهما بعثنا عليكم عبادا لنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the phrase about a seated recorder on the right and left, the wording relies on the second side to supply the first by ellipsis.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قوله: عن اليمين وعن الشمال قعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The compressed wording means: would you exhaust yourself in grief over the person who was made to see his evil deed as good? The following clause resumes that thought.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أفمن زين له سوء عمله فرآه حسنا، ذهبت نفسك حسرة عليه؟! فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات

words: إلا من ظلم ثم بدل حسنا بعد سوء
rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra takes the exception as implicit: messengers do not fear, while others do, except a wrongdoer who repents, who need not fear.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الفراء، وهو يبعد: لأن العرب إنما تحذف من الكلام ما يدل عليه ما يظهر

words: إلا من ظلم ثم بدل حسنا بعد سوء
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba rejects al-Farra's ellipsis because Arabic omits only what the expressed wording indicates, and this reading lacks such a cue.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الفراء، وهو يبعد: لأن العرب إنما تحذف من الكلام ما يدل عليه ما يظهر

words: إلا من ظلم ثم بدل حسنا بعد سوء
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses first fears the serpent, then God reassures him; the exception addresses his further fear over killing a man, which repentance and regret can remove.
rows.anchor: قال أبو محمد: والذي عندي فيه، والله أعلم، أن موسى عليه السلام، لما خاف الثعبان وولى ولم يعقب

words: إلا من ظلم ثم بدل حسنا بعد سوء
rows.speaker: بعض النحويين
rows.claim: Some grammarians understand illa here as wa-la, giving the sense “nor the one who did wrong”; they compare the construction with the exception in 2:150.
rows.anchor: وبعض النحويين يحمل (إلا من ظلم) بمعنى: ولا من ظلم، كقوله: لئلا يكون للناس عليكم حجة إلا الذين ظلموا منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He compares this discourse returning to an earlier implied topic with 8:5: that verse resumes the sura's earlier subject rather than comparing the two stories directly.
rows.anchor: ولم يشبه قصة المؤمنين بإخراج الله إياه، ولكن الكلام مردود إلى معنى في أول السورة ومحمول عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Badr, the Prophet saw Muslim reluctance and few numbers, offered rewards for kills and captives, and some objected and disputed; the sura then addressed the spoils.
rows.anchor: رأى يوم بدر قلة المسلمين وكراهة كثير منهم للقتال، فنفل كل امرئ منهم ما أصاب، وجعل لكل من قتل قتيلا كذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the account of the man coming from the city's outskirts, saʿy means hurrying on foot and can also mean running.
rows.anchor: أي يسرع في مشيه، وهو العدو أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿy can mean walking, and it can also mean helping someone with his undertaking.
rows.anchor: يعني المشي، ويقال: المعاونة له على أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to hasten to God's remembrance means to walk there.
rows.anchor: وقال: فاسعوا إلى ذكر الله

rows.speaker: بعض السلف
rows.claim: Some early authorities read “فامضوا إلى ذكر الله” in place of “فاسعوا إلى ذكر الله,” consistent with the sense “walk.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض السلف: فامضوا إلى ذكر الله

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some exegetes take the birds coming to Abraham “saʿyan” to mean that they came walking.
rows.anchor: أي مشيا، كذلك قال بعض المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿy can mean work or action: seeking the afterlife with its saʿy means doing the work it requires.
rows.anchor: والسعي: العمل، قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the phrase about those striving against God's signs, saʿy means exerting oneself diligently.
rows.anchor: والذين سعوا في آياتنا معاجزين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The differing saʿy of people means their deeds differ.
rows.anchor: أي عملكم لشتى، أي مختلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common underlying sense of saʿy is walking and moving quickly.
rows.anchor: وأصل هذا كله: المشي والإسراع فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farah first means joy or gladness, as in people rejoicing in a favorable wind at sea.
rows.anchor: الفرح: المسرة، قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farah can also mean satisfaction, since satisfaction follows from gladness; the cited groups are content with what they have.
rows.anchor: والفرح: الرضا، لأنه عن المسرة يكون، قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farah can mean arrogant exultation or insolence, an excess of joy; this is the sense in the verse about those whom God does not love.
rows.anchor: والفرح: البطر والأشر، لأن ذلك عن إفراط السرور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this sense, ḥāʾ may alternate with hāʾ: fārihīn means insolent and arrogant, and the consonants are close in articulation, as in madaḥtuhu/madahtuhu.
rows.anchor: وقد تبدل (الحاء) في هذا المعنى (هاء) فيقال: فره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those waging war against God and the Messenger are people who rebel against the ruler and Muslim community, terrorize roads, and spread corruption.
rows.anchor: المحاربون لله ورسوله: هم الخارجون على الإمام وعلى جماعة المسلمين، يخيفون السبل، ويسعون في الأرض بالفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author divides offenders into three classes: killing without taking property, killing and taking property, and taking property without killing.
rows.anchor: وهم ثلاثة أصناف: رجل قتل النفس ولم يأخذ مالا. ورجل قتل النفس وأخذ المال. ورجل أخذ المال ولم يقتل النفس

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One legal view gives the ruler discretion to apply any of the listed punishments to any offender class.
rows.anchor: فإذا قدر الإمام عليهم فإن بعضهم يقول: هو مخير في هذه العقوبات، بأيها شاء عاقب كل صنف منهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Under a view assigning a fixed penalty to each class, a killer who took no property is executed, because life is exchanged for life.
rows.anchor: وكان بعضهم يجعل لكل صنف منهم حدا لا يتجاوزه إلى غيره: فمن قتل النفس ولم يأخذ المال قتل، لأن النفس بالنفس

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Under that fixed-penalty view, a killer who also took property is crucified until death: crucifixion answers the theft and death answers the killing.
rows.anchor: ومن قتل وأخذ المال: صلب إلى أن يموت، فكان الشهر له بالصلب جزاء له بأخذه المال

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: For taking property without killing, this view permits cutting the right hand for theft and left foot for public violence, or banishing the offender.
rows.anchor: ومن أصاب المال ولم يقتل، فإن شاء الإمام قطع يده اليمنى جزاء بالسرق، ورجله اليسرى جزاء بالخروج

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One interpretation of banishment is that people should be ordered to kill the offender if they encounter him.
rows.anchor: وقد اختلفوا في نفيه من الأرض، فقال بعضهم: هو أن يقال: من لقيه فليقتله

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: Another interpretation of banishment is searching for the offender wherever he may be.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: هو أن يطلب في كل أرض يكون بها

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: A further interpretation of banishment is expelling the offender from his home town.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: هو أن ينفى من بلده

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation equates banishment with imprisonment.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: هو أن يحبس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba prefers imprisonment as the closest sense of banishment: a prisoner cannot travel through the lands and is confined to one place.
rows.anchor: ولا أرى شيئا من هذه التفاسير، أشبه بالنفي في هذا الموضع من الحبس، لأنه إذا حبس ومنع من التصرف

rows.speaker: بعض المسجونين
rows.claim: A prisoners' poem depicts confinement as exclusion from the world: its speakers are neither alive nor dead, and marvel when the jailer visits.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المسجونين : خرجنا من الدنيا ونحن من أهلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kill-on-sight and perpetual-pursuit readings seem to make banishment a pre-capture punishment, since the ruler cannot catch and release the offender just to order a later killing or search.
rows.anchor: ومن جعل النفي له أن يقال: من لقيه فليقتله، أو أن يطلب في كل أرض يكون بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “We created them except in truth,” the preposition bi serves in the place of li, so the phrase means “for the sake of truth.”
rows.anchor: قال الله تعالى: ما خلقناهما إلا بالحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the hadith comparing people to a hundred camels, the hundred means a herd gathered at pasture and is also called hunayda; a riding camel stands out by maturity and appearance.
rows.anchor: الإبل المائة: هي الراعية، وإنما يجتمع منها في المرعى الواحد مائة، فتقام المائة مقام القطيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel comparison means people are equal under law and in retaliation; rank gives no one an advantage. The author links it with the comb-teeth saying and an Arab donkey-teeth proverb.
rows.anchor: فأراد: أنهم سواء في الأحكام وفي القصاص، ليس لشريف فضل على غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥabaṭ is a camel's belly swelling after it eats too much pasture; yulam means that it nearly kills.
rows.anchor: فالحبط: أن تأكل الناقة في المرعي فتكثر حتى تنتفخ بطنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's warning about spring growth illustrates avoiding excess worldly abundance and beauty when they can prove destructive, like an animal overeating grass.
rows.anchor: وإنما نهى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن الاستكثار من الدنيا ومن غضارتها وحسنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction to settle in a house like a gazelle means to stay quietly without doing anything, like a gazelle settled in its lair.
rows.anchor: يراد: أقم ولا تحدث شيئا كأنك ظبي قد استقر في الكناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Clothed yet naked” women are those wearing thin garments that do not cover them.
rows.anchor: يعني النساء اللواتي يلبسن رقاق الثياب، فهن كاسيات إذا لبسن، عاريات إذا كن لا يسترهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a peace document, a “closed bag” means a heart clear of rancor and committed to fidelity; Arabs call the chests ʿiyāb, as an unnamed poet confirms.
rows.anchor: يريد: صدرا نقيا من الغل والعداوة، منطويا على الوفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author discusses poetic rhyme defects, including raising one rhyme vowel and lowering another, and repeating the same rhyme twice.
rows.anchor: وخالف في الإكفاء بأن رفع قافية وخفض أخرى. وخالف في الإبطاء بأن أعاد قافية مرتين

rows.speaker: ابن الرقاع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Riqāʿ describes revising a poem by collecting it, correcting its crookedness and sanad, and straightening it like a lance.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الرقاع يذكر تنقيحه شعره

rows.speaker: ذو الرمة
rows.claim: Dhu al-Rumma describes a rare poem whose rhymes avoid sanad and muḥāl.
rows.anchor: وقال ذو الرمة : وشعر قد أرقت له غريب

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda defines iqwāʾ as raising one rhyme vowel and lowering another.
rows.anchor: هذا قول أبي عبيدة. وبعضهم يجعل الإقواء رفع قافية وجر أخرى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another definition of iqwāʾ is raising one rhyme ending and making another genitive.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم يجعل الإقواء رفع قافية وجر أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba prefers Abu ʿUbayda's account because iqwāʾ derives from quwwa, a strand of rope; losing a metrical part is like losing a strand.
rows.anchor: وقول أبي عبيدة أجود عندي لأن الإقواء من القوة، والقوة: طاقة من الحبل

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited line “when she saw the colostrum milk drunk” exemplifies a missing element in the verse; “مشروبة” would make it regular.
rows.anchor: لما رأت ماء السلا مشروبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic Arabic uses many rhetorical modes, including metaphor, analogy, inversion, fronting, ellipsis, repetition, concealment, explicitness, allusion, and shifts in number and address.
rows.anchor: وللعرب المجازات في الكلام، ومعناها: طرق القول ومآخذه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Qur'anic expression uses the full range of Arabic figurative speech, no translator can transfer it into another language as the earlier scriptural books were translated.
rows.anchor: وبكل هذه المذاهب نزل القرآن ولذلك لا يقدر أحد من التراجم على أن ينقله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The compressed command means that if a treaty partner's betrayal is feared, one must notify them that the pact is ended and announce war so both sides know equally.
rows.anchor: إن كان بينك وبين قوم هدنة وعهد، فخفت منهم خيانة ونقضا

words: لَّا يُسْـَٔلُ عَن ذَنۢبِهِۦٓ إِنسٌۭ وَلَا جَآنٌّۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses are reconciled by stages in the long Day of Judgment: people are questioned at presentation, then after the case is settled speech and dispute end, faces are marked, and books are distributed.
rows.anchor: ففي مثل هذا اليوم يسألون وفيه لا يسألون، لأنهم حين يعرضون يوقفون على الذنوب ويحاسبون

words: لَّا يُسْـَٔلُ عَن ذَنۢبِهِۦٓ إِنسٌۭ وَلَا جَآنٌّۭ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse describes one particular station at which people are not questioned.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that criminals are not asked about their sins in the Qarun passage expresses the same stage-specific point.
rows.anchor: ومثله: ولا يسئل عن ذنوبهم المجرمون

words: ثم إنكم يوم القيامة عند ربكم تختصمون
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People first dispute and the wronged accuse oppressors; after retribution and judgment, they are told that further argument, speech, or excuses will do them no good.
rows.anchor: لأنهم يختصمون ويدعي المظلومون على الظالمين، ففي تلك الحال يختصمون

words: ثم إنكم يوم القيامة عند ربكم تختصمون
rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima explains that there are several stations: people speak and quarrel at one, then God seals their mouths and their hands and feet speak, after which they cannot speak.
rows.anchor: فقال: إنها مواقف، فأما موقف منها: فتكلموا واختصموا

words: ويكأن الله يبسط الرزق لمن يشاء
rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī takes waykaʾanna to mean “Have you not seen?” in both occurrences in the verse.
rows.anchor: فقال الكسائي: معناها: ألم تر

words: ويكأن الله يبسط الرزق لمن يشاء
rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda explains it as “does he not know that God gives provision abundantly to whom He wills,” supporting al-Kisāʾī's interpretation.
rows.anchor: وروى عبد الرزاق، عن معمر، عن قتادة أنه قال

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl parses the form as two words: way, followed by a new clause beginning kaʾanna Allāh.
rows.anchor: وذكر الخليل أنها مفصولة: وي، ثم تبتدئ فتقول: كأن الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In the report through Abū Ṣāliḥ, Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as kaʾanna Allāh and kaʾannahu lā yufliḥu, treating way as a connective filler; this supports al-Khalīl.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس في رواية أبي صالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form's ability to be lightened like kaʾanna supports construing it as kaʾanna.
rows.anchor: ومما يدل على أنها كأن: أنها قد تخفف أيضا كما تخفف كأن

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's line uses the form in a way that can be read as kaʾanna: a wealthy person is loved while the poor live harshly.
rows.anchor: كما تخفف كأن قال الشاعر .

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view takes waykaʾanna to mean “mercy upon you” in the language of Ḥimyar.
rows.anchor: وقال (بعضهم) : ويكأن: أي رحمة لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalq can mean fabrication or conjectural lying: the source explains the phrases in 26:137 and 29:17 that way and equates ikhtilāq with invented falsehood.
rows.anchor: الخلق: التخرص، قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalq also means forming or shaping, as in shaping clay into the likeness of a bird.
rows.anchor: والخلق: التصوير، قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalq can mean bringing into being or initiating creation.
rows.anchor: والخلق: الإنشاء والابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The underlying sense of khalq is measuring or determining; the leather-cutter shapes what he then cuts, as Zuhayr's verse illustrates.
rows.anchor: قال زهير : ولأنت تفري ما خلقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalq can mean religion: “no change to God's khalq” means no change to God's religion.
rows.anchor: والخلق: الدين، كقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to alter God's khalq may refer to changing religion, or to bodily practices such as castration and slitting ears.
rows.anchor: أي دينه: ويقال: تغيير خلقه بالخصاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basic Arab sense of ẓulm is placing something outside its proper place; common expressions apply it to resemblance, premature drinking, needless slaughter, wrongly dug land, and leaving a road.
rows.anchor: في كلام العرب: وضع الشيء في غير موضعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓulm can mean shirk because assigning God a partner places lordship where it does not belong; this is also the sense of the cited verse in al-Anʿām.
rows.anchor: ثم قد يصير الظلم بمعنى الشرك، لأن من جعل لله شريكا: فقد وضع الربوبية غير موضعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓulm also means diminution or withholding: the cited phrases about crops, rights, and souls mean that nothing was reduced or withheld.
rows.anchor: ويكون الظلم: النقصان، قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓulm can mean denial: the Thamūd denied that the she-camel was from God, and “wronging Our signs” means denying them.
rows.anchor: ويكون الظلم: الجحد، قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raising al-ṣābiʾūn is defended as coordination with the nominative syntactic position of the opening phrase after inna, which the author says adds no meaning-changing force.
rows.anchor: رفع (الصابئين) لأنه رد على موضع إن الذين آمنوا وموضعه رفع، لأن (إن) مبتدأة وليست تحدث في الكلام معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike inna, laʿalla introduces doubt; therefore the author contrasts a raised conjunct after inna with an accusative conjunct after laʿalla.
rows.anchor: وتقول: زيد قائم، ثم تقول: ليت زيدا قائم، فتحدث في الكلام معنى الشك

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī permits coordination that leaves both nouns nominative with inna, as well as a singular predicate with the coordinated subject.
rows.anchor: وكان الكسائي يجيز: أن عبد الله وزيد قائمان، وإن عبد الله وزيد قائم

rows.speaker: البصريون
rows.claim: The Basrans also allow the construction and cite “Indeed God and His angels bless the Prophet” as an example.
rows.anchor: والبصريون يجيزونه، ويحكون: إن الله وملائكته يصلون على النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous poem coordinating “Qiyār” with the first-person subject after inna supports the construction.
rows.anchor: وينشدون : فمن يك أمسى بالمدينة رحله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One explanation of the accusative “those who establish prayer” supplies an implied preposition: what was sent down to you and to them.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم: أراد بما أنزل إليك وإلى المقيمين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation supplies “from before them,” connecting the phrase to what was sent down previously.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: وما أنزل من قبلك ومن قبل المقيمين

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī connects the accusative to “they believe in what was sent down to you,” taking it to mean belief in those who establish prayer; he compares “believes for the believers.”
rows.anchor: وكان الكسائي يرده إلى قوله: يؤمنون بما أنزل إليك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some treat the accusative as an accusative of praise.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: هو نصب على المدح

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda attributes the accusative to the length of the coordinated construction and cites al-Khirniq's poem with an accusative participle.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة : هو نصب على تطاول الكلام بالنسق

rows.speaker: عاصم الجحدري
rows.claim: All readers recite al-ṣābirīn in the accusative except ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī, who recited it nominative but wrote it accusative, following the earlier grammatical rationale.
rows.anchor: والقراء جميعا على نصب الصابرين إلا عاصما الجحدري فإنه كان يرفع الحرف إذا قرأه، وينصبه إذا كتبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anā can mean “how,” as in the question about how God will revive the town and the instruction to approach the field as one wishes.
rows.anchor: أني: يكون بمعنيين. يكون بمعنى: كيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anā can also mean “from where,” as in the questions about the source of God's child and how disbelievers are turned away.
rows.anchor: وتكون بمعنى: من أين، نحو قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two senses are close enough that either may be interpreted through the other; al-Kumayt's line explicitly uses both “anā” and “min ayna.”
rows.anchor: وقال الكميت : أنى ومن أين آبك الطرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no contradiction between people conversing in one passage and not asking one another in another: at the first trumpet blast, kinship ends, each is occupied with himself, and people swoon; after the next blast they rise and converse.
rows.anchor: فإنه إذا نفخ في الصور نفخة واحدة، تقطعت الأرحام، وبطلت الأنساب، وشغلوا بأنفسهم عن التسآل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is cited as holding the same staged explanation of when people ask one another.
rows.anchor: وهو معنى قول ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth was created first in two days; the heavens, then smoke, were made in two; afterward God spread and anchored the gathered earth and grew its plants in two, totaling six days.
rows.anchor: فابتدأ الخلق للأرض على ما في الآي الأول في يومين، ثم خلق السموات وكانت دخانا في يومين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “After that He spread it” does not mean that earth was first created then; daha means that He spread and extended it after its initial creation.
rows.anchor: وإنما كان يجد الطاعن متعلقا ومقالا لو قال: والأرض بعد ذلك خلقها أو ابتدأها أو أنشأها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says “after that” here means “together with that,” noting that the Arabs can use “with” and “after” equivalently.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : بعد ذلك في هذا الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The differing food descriptions are reconciled by the Fire's levels and the Garden's grades: punishment and reward vary with people's sins and good deeds, so different inhabitants receive different food and drink.
rows.anchor: فإن النار دركات، والجنة درجات، وعلى قدر الذنوب والحسنات تقع العقوبات والمثوبات
